claim: Arge 1996 (buffer tree) describes a search tree whose internal nodes have fan-out Theta(m) and a buffer of Theta(m) blocks each, where an update is a time-stamped message put in the root buffer and pushed one level down only when a buffer runs full (m = blocks that fit in memory).

Arge 1996 (buffer tree) assumes one process drives the whole tree (a batched, offline model), memory holds m blocks, and a buffer is read and written as a sorted whole in one pass; no concurrency is treated.
Brodal and Fagerberg 2003 give lower bounds from an adversary argument, and three matching upper bounds: truncated buffer trees, B-trees with buffers, and B-trees.
Brodal and Fagerberg 2003 assume comparison-based external memory, one operation at a time, a fixed block size B, and update cost counted amortised.

Bender and others 2015 (B-epsilon-tree introduction): compared with a B-tree, batching messages divides the insertion cost by the batch size B^(1-epsilon); for the paper's example B = 1024 and epsilon = 1/2 a B-epsilon-tree can perform inserts 16 times faster than a B-tree.

Bender and others 2015: on a file-system benchmark that creates 3 million 200-byte files in a balanced directory tree, the steady-state performance of BetrFS is an order of magnitude faster than the other file systems.
Bender and others 2015 state that an upsert message can accelerate updates by one to two orders of magnitude without slowing down queries.
Bender and others 2015: internal nodes keep part of their space as a message buffer, and messages (insert, tombstone, upsert) enter at the root and move down in batches when a buffer is full.
Bender and others 2015 assume nodes are large (about 4 MB), so the I/O cost of a flush is amortised, and that messages are small relative to the batch.
Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS): a kernel file system whose metadata and data live in two B-epsilon-trees, where every small write is an upsert message into the root buffer.
Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS): on one microdata benchmark, BetrFS provides more than 4x the performance of ext4 or XFS.
Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS): an in-place rsync of the Linux kernel source realizes roughly 1.6-22x speedup over other commodity file systems.

Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS): 1,000 random 4-byte writes within a 1GiB file, followed by an fsync(), took 0.17 s on BetrFS against 11.60, 11.71, 11.60 and 14.75 s on the four other file systems (4-core machine), and the paper says BetrFS was two orders of magnitude faster.

Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS): in a worked model of 1TB with 128-byte keys and records, a branching factor of 10 and 1MB nodes, a B-epsilon-tree inserts data 14.3 times faster than a B-tree (a worked calculation in the paper, not a benchmark).
Jannen and others 2015 (BetrFS) assume large nodes (1 MB in the model, 4 MB in the system), small items, a mostly-write workload, and disks where a seek dominates.
O'Neil and others 1996 (LSM-tree; analytic, no running system): typically the product of the two ratios gives a cost ratio improvement of nearly two orders of magnitude.

O'Neil and others 1996 (LSM-tree; analytic, no running system): COST_LSM-ins / COST_B-ins = K1 * (COST/COSTP) * (1/M), with K1 approximately 0.67, COST/COSTP the cost of a page in a multi-page block against a random page I/O, and M the average number of C0 entries inserted into one C1 leaf per merge; the example ratio is 0.02 = 1/50.
O'Neil and others 1996 (LSM-tree; analytic, no running system): the introduction states the gain as 'at an order of magnitude lower cost'.

O'Neil and others 1996 (LSM-tree): inserts go to a memory tree C0 with no I/O, and a rolling merge moves ranges of entries into a disk tree C1 (and further into C2 ... CK) in multi-page blocks, deferring and batching the work.

O'Neil and others 1996 (LSM-tree) assume a disk where a multi-page block is cheaper per page than a random page (ratio about 1/10), memory for C0, a steady insert rate, and that entries are rarely deleted before reaching the last component.
Luo and Carey 2020 (LSM survey; no own measurement): the write cost is O(T * L / B) for leveling and O(L / B) for tiering.

Luo and Carey 2020 (LSM survey) assume write cost is I/O of page-sized blocks, memory large enough for the buffer, and Bloom filters for point lookups.

claim: Dayan and Idreos 2018 (Dostoevsky): lazy leveling merges only at the largest level, with tiering at the smaller levels; in the Fluid LSM-tree, K = 1 and Z = 1 gives leveling, K = Z = T - 1 gives tiering, and K = T - 1 with Z = 1 gives lazy leveling.

Dayan and Idreos 2018: lazy leveling (1) improves the cost complexity of updates, (2) keeps the same complexity for point lookups, long range lookups and space amplification, and (3) gives competitive performance for short range lookups; the text states no single speed-up number.

Dayan and Idreos 2018: with lazy leveling an updated entry takes O(1) merge operations per level across levels 1 to L-1 and O(T) at level L, so O(L + T) merge operations per entry, divided by the block size B, against O(T*L) for leveling.

Dayan and Idreos 2018: in their evaluation (inserting 1TB of data into an empty database, each entry 1KB), the update cost with lazy leveling scales at a slower rate than with leveling as the data size grows.

claim: Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992 (log-structured file system): changes are buffered in memory and written as one long sequential segment, and a cleaner later copies the live data out of old segments.

Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992: the log-structured file system outperforms current Unix file systems by an order of magnitude for small-file writes, while matching or exceeding Unix performance for reads and large writes.
Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992: even when the overhead for cleaning is included, Sprite LFS can use 70% of the disk bandwidth for writing, whereas Unix file systems typically can use only 5-10%.
Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992 assume a sequential write is much cheaper than a seek, reads are served from cache, and a cleaner keeps clean segments available.

Buchsbaum and others 2000 (a two-page abstract on external memory graph traversal): the buffered repository tree is a tree whose internal nodes each hold a buffer, and inserts go to the root buffer and move down when a buffer overflows.
Buchsbaum and others 2000 assume the root lives in memory and each buffer holds one block of items.
